title: Why Gym Memberships Are Designed for You to Quit
sources: Planet Fitness, Inc., Form 10-K for fiscal year 2025 (SEC EDGAR, filed 2026): approximately 20.8 million members and 2,896 clubs at year-end 2025 (~7,200 members/club, derived: 20.8M ÷ 2,896); Classic Card $15/month, PF Black Card $24.99/month (rising to $29.99 after 2026 peak join season), $49 standard annual fee

DellaVigna & Malmendier, 'Paying Not to Go to the Gym', American Economic Review 96(3), 2006: 7,752 members across 3 U.S. health clubs over 3 years; monthly-contract members averaged ~4.3 visits/month, a real cost of $17+ per visit vs. a $10 per-visit pass; ~80% of monthly members would have saved money on a pay-per-visit contract, forgoing average savings of $600-700/year

Industry survey compilations (Health & Fitness Association-sourced data via Gymdesk/Glofox/smarthealthclubs.com, 2025-2026, soft/secondary source): ~67% of gym members rarely or never use their membership; Americans waste an estimated $1.3 billion/year on unused memberships; ~66% annual retention (roughly 1 in 3 members cancel yearly); about half of new members quit within 6 months

Strava year-end data / 'Quitter's Day': analysis of 30M+ global January activities identifies the second Friday of January (Jan 9, 2026) as the day resolution activity drops sharply; ~80% of resolutions abandoned by that point
Gym industry survey compilations (GymMaster/Glofox, 2025-2026): ~12% of a year's gym sign-ups happen in January; check-ins rise ~30-50% in the first two weeks of January vs. December

LA Fitness membership agreement / cancellation policy (company FAQ, lafitnessmembership.com): written cancellation required, 30 days' notice, mailed (certified mail recommended) to a PO box, or in person
Planet Fitness cancellation policy (company FAQ): cancel in person at home club or by mail; request must arrive several business days before the billing date or another month is billed

FTC, 'Negative Option Rule' ('click-to-cancel'): finalized Oct 2024, was to take effect July 14, 2025; the Eighth Circuit vacated it July 8, 2025 for a procedural (Reg Flex Act) violation; FTC submitted a draft ANPRM to OIRA Jan 30, 2026 to restart rulemaking (not yet law as of this video); state auto-renewal laws (e.g. CA, NY, MN) separately require easy cancellation
ClassPass pricing pages (2026): pay-per-class/credit membership model, plans roughly $19-$249/month by city and credit count, no long-term contract required

alt_titles: The Gym Business Model: Why They Want You to Quit
Why Cancelling a Gym Is Harder Than Joining One
youtube.hook: Why do gyms want you to sign up and never show up? A famous study found most members would save money paying per visit instead. Dave signs a gym contract on January 1st, goes three times, and keeps paying all year. We break down why: Planet Fitness has about 7,200 members per club (way more than any floor holds), the January sign-up spike and 'Quitter's Day' drop-off, the famous DellaVigna & Malmendier study proving most monthly members would save money paying per visit, the psychology (present bias) behind why smart people still sign long contracts, the hard-to-cancel tactics (certified mail, in-person only, 30-day notice), and the FTC's 'click-to-cancel' rule that got vacated by a federal court in 2025. Then, practical ways to avoid the trap: pay-per-visit apps, month-to-month plans, and an honest 'will I actually go' test before you sign.

beats.text: This is me on January first signing a gym contract and promising myself I will go every single day.
March. I've been three times. And the gym doesn't call me. The gym doesn't care.
Because I'm still paying them every single month for a gym I never visit.
Turns out that's not an accident. It's the plan.
By the end of this video you'll know the one number every gym hopes you never figure out and it takes ten seconds.
But most people click off before that part which is exactly what the gym wants.
So let me show you the business I actually signed up for.
Planet Fitness has about seven thousand members for every one of its clubs. Seven thousand people per building.
That's not a gym. That's a stadium with a membership card.
Now picture seven thousand people waiting for one squat rack.
A normal gym floor fits maybe two or three hundred people at once. Not seven thousand.
So how does that work? Simple. The gym is betting that almost nobody shows up. And most months most members show up zero times.
It's like a buffet that only stays open because most people don't come hungry. If everyone ate the buffet would go broke by Tuesday.
Including me. I'm most members.
It's like an airline that sells three hundred tickets for a plane with one hundred seats and just hopes you oversleep.
Me paying for a gym I don't go to.
And the cheap price is the whole trick. It costs less than my coffee habit so I never feel the pain enough to cancel.
Ten dollars a month doesn't feel like money. Until you count how many months.
And the gym knows exactly when to catch me. January.
New year new me. Everybody signs up in the same two weeks. For a gym January is like October for a pumpkin farm.
And I was one of them. I posted my membership card online with a flexing emoji. Thirty eight likes. Peak of my fitness career.
The place is packed. There's a line for the treadmill. A guy is filming himself doing curls in the squat rack.
The parking lot is full. People are parking on the grass. It feels like a concert except everyone is sweating for no reason.
Me in the first week of January.
I tell my neighbor Bob I'm a changed man. I buy the shaker bottle and the gloves and the tiny towel.
And the gym prints my card and smiles. Because they've seen this exact movie every January and they know how it ends.
Think about it. Does the gym hire more staff in January? Nope. Do they buy more treadmills? Nope. They just wait.
There's even a day for when it all falls apart.
A fitness app looked at millions of workouts and found the exact day people give up. They call it Quitter's Day.
It's the second Friday of January. Not March. Not even February. The second Friday of January.
Not even two weeks. My New Year's resolution had a shorter life than a carton of milk.
My motivation on the second Friday of January.
That was me. I went three times. Then it rained once and I took it personally.
And everybody who signed up with me? Same. The gym gets quieter every week but the money keeps coming in.
And every month a little message from my bank. Gym membership. Paid. Like a tiny reminder that I'm a liar.
By March the only guy still going was the one filming himself.
So I did something no gym member should ever do. I did the math.
Here's the one number. Take what you pay every month and divide it by how many times you actually went.
For me it was thirty dollars a visit. For one shower basically. The most expensive shower of my life.
I could have hired a personal trainer to come to my house and yell at me for less money.
My gym membership versus my actual workouts.
And this isn't just me being lazy. Two economists studied thousands of real gym members and found the same thing.
People on the monthly plan paid way more per visit than if they just bought a ten visit pass. Most of them would have saved hundreds a year.
Read that again. The people who picked the monthly plan to save money lost money. Because they bet on the wrong version of themselves.
So basically we paid extra for the right to feel guilty about not going.
The gym business model in one picture.
Now you might think this only happens to lazy people. Nope. It happens to you too.
There are two of me. Tonight me just wants pizza. But January me is sure that future me will run every morning.
And January me is the one who signs the contract. Every time.
The gym isn't selling to you. It's selling to January you. The most optimistic person who has ever lived.
Future me after January me signs a twelve month contract.
It's the same reason people buy a treadmill and it turns into the most expensive clothes rack in the house.
Me hanging a shirt on a treadmill I paid nine hundred dollars for.
Be honest. You have a treadmill or a yoga mat or a bike somewhere holding laundry right now.
So in April I decide I'm done. Time to cancel.
Signing up took me two minutes on my phone. Cancelling? Different story.
Some big gyms want a written letter. Sent by mail. With thirty days notice. Like I'm resigning from a job in nineteen fifty.
I had to buy a stamp. I didn't even know what a stamp costs anymore. I had to Google it.
Me at the post office trying to quit a gym.
Other gyms make you cancel in person at your home club. And if you show up on the wrong day you get billed again.
My friend Kevin tried to cancel in person. They told him the manager who handles cancellations works Tuesdays. Only Tuesdays.
Netflix? Two taps and you're out. Nobody asks you to mail a letter to Netflix.
The gym front desk when I say the word cancel.
And the crazy part? The government actually tried to fix this.
There was a rule called click to cancel. If you can sign up online you have to be able to cancel online. Simple.
It was supposed to start in the summer of twenty twenty five. And days before it did a court threw it out.
Gym owners reading that court news.
So right now it depends on where you live. Some states already make gyms let you cancel easily and some don't.
Some of those state laws even say if you joined online they have to let you leave online. So look up your state before you buy a single stamp.
Gyms when that rule got thrown out.
And honestly? Part of me gets it.
If all seven thousand members showed up on the same Monday the gym would explode. The building only works because people like me stay home.
Imagine every single member showing up on Monday at six. People doing pushups in the parking lot.
So in a weird way my empty spot on the treadmill is paying for someone else's workout.
That doesn't make the cancel maze okay. It just means the gym isn't selling workouts. It's selling the feeling of being someone who works out.
So here's how I play it now. Quick reminder this is education and not advice.
Before I sign anything I ask last year me. Not January me. How many times did I actually work out last year?
If the honest answer is not much I pay per visit first. A day pass costs more one time but way less than a year of guilt.
Or try the free stuff first. A park and some stairs and your own two legs. If you can't show up for free you won't show up for thirty a month.
If I do sign up I pick month to month even if it costs a bit more. I'm paying for the exit door.
I put my gym days in my calendar like a meeting with my boss. Because I skip workouts but I don't skip my boss.
And once a year I check my bank statement for anything still charging me. Gym included. It takes fifteen minutes.
Last time I did it I found a gym and two streaming apps and a magazine I forgot I was paying for. A magazine.
And when I finally cancelled? Certified mail. Receipt. A screenshot of the tracking page. Paper trails win arguments.
Me walking out of the post office with my receipt.
So remember that one number. What you pay divided by how many times you go.
If that number is bigger than a day pass the gym isn't your gym. You're the customer who never comes.
And if it's smaller? Congrats. You're the rare person the gym actually loses money on. Keep going.
The gym doesn't make money when you work out. It makes money when you don't.
Next time my dog needs surgery and the bill nearly knocks me over. We'll find out why vet bills got so crazy.
Subscribe. It's free and it's way easier to cancel than a gym.
